`ln`: make links between files.

## Synopsis

<strong>ln</strong> \[<strong>-sfnv</strong>\] <em>target</em> \[<em>link</em>\]\
<strong>ln</strong> \[<strong>-sfnv</strong>\] <em>target</em>... <em>directory</em>

## Description

In the first form, <strong>ln</strong> makes a link named <em>link</em> to <em>target</em>. With no <em>link</em>, the link is made in the current directory with the target's last name. If <em>link</em> is an existing directory, the link goes inside it, as in the second form.

In the second form, <strong>ln</strong> makes a link to each <em>target</em> inside <em>directory</em>, each named after its target's last name.

Without <strong>-s</strong>, <strong>ln</strong> makes a hard link, which no filesystem in mcos supports: it always fails with "Operation not permitted".

## Options

Options must come before the first operand; they may be combined (<strong>-sf</strong>).

<strong>-s</strong>
: Make symbolic links. The target is stored as given; a relative target is followed from the link's directory, not from where <strong>ln</strong> ran.

<strong>-f</strong>
: Remove an existing file or link of the link's name first.

<strong>-n</strong>
: Treat a last operand that is a symbolic link to a directory as a name, not as a directory to put links in (with <strong>-f</strong>, it is replaced).

<strong>-v</strong>
: Print each link made, as <em>link</em> -\> <em>target</em>, each name in single quotes.

## Exit status

0 if every link was made; 1 if any failed, on a bad option, a missing operand, or several targets and a last operand that is not a directory.

## Examples

```text
ln -s /mnt/sata/1/notes notes
ln -sf ../lib/new.lua lib.lua
ln -s /bin/ls /bin/cat /tmp
```

## See also

<strong>ls</strong>(1), <strong>rm</strong>(1), <strong>cp</strong>(1), <strong>mv</strong>(1)
